subject: biology
title: Molecular genetics
summary: Explains the enzymes of DNA replication, transcription and translation in detail, gene regulation in prokaryotes (the lac operon) and eukaryotes, and the types of mutation and their effects on proteins.
body:
Mendel described what is inherited; molecular genetics explains how. DNA is copied each time a cell divides, and its information is read out as RNA and then protein, the flow of information often called the **central dogma**. Cells also control which genes are read and when. Understanding these steps explains how antibiotics such as streptomycin target bacterial ribosomes, how a single base change can cause disease, and how biotechnology tools such as PCR work.

## Key ideas

### DNA replication

Replication is **semi-conservative**: each new double helix contains one original (parental) strand and one newly made strand. Meselson and Stahl showed this in 1958 by growing bacteria in heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N), switching them to light nitrogen (¹⁴N) and separating DNA by density: after one generation all DNA was of intermediate density, and after two generations half was intermediate and half light.

Replication starts at **origins of replication**. Bacteria have one origin on their circular chromosome; eukaryotes have many along each linear chromosome so the large genome can be copied in time. Replication moves outward in both directions from each origin, forming two **replication forks**.

The key proteins at a fork:

| Protein | Role |
|---|---|
| **Helicase** | Unwinds the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between bases |
| **Single-strand binding proteins** | Coat separated strands to stop them re-pairing |
| **Topoisomerase** | Relieves the twisting strain ahead of the fork by cutting and rejoining DNA |
| **Primase** | Makes a short RNA **primer** to provide a starting 3′ end |
| **DNA polymerase III** (bacteria) | Main enzyme adding nucleotides to the 3′ end; also proofreads |
| **DNA polymerase I** (bacteria) | Removes RNA primers and replaces them with DNA |
| **DNA ligase** | Seals the gaps in the sugar–phosphate backbone |

(Eukaryotes use different DNA polymerases, mainly δ and ε, but the jobs are the same.)

All DNA polymerases can only add nucleotides to a free **3′–OH group**, so new DNA is always made **5′ → 3′**. Because the two template strands are antiparallel:

- The **leading strand** is made continuously, toward the fork.
- The **lagging strand** is made discontinuously, away from the fork, in short pieces called **Okazaki fragments** (about 1000–2000 nucleotides in bacteria, and much shorter in eukaryotes), each started with its own primer and later joined by ligase.

Accuracy is high because DNA polymerase checks each newly added base and removes mismatches (**proofreading**, using 3′ → 5′ exonuclease activity), and **mismatch repair** enzymes fix most remaining errors after replication.

### Transcription

**Transcription** copies a gene's DNA sequence into RNA. **RNA polymerase** binds a **promoter**, unwinds the DNA and builds RNA 5′ → 3′ by reading the **template strand** (also called the antisense strand) 3′ → 5′. The RNA has the same sequence as the other DNA strand, the **coding strand**, except that U replaces T. RNA polymerase needs no primer.

- In **bacteria**, a **sigma factor** helps RNA polymerase recognise the promoter (with conserved sequences about 10 and 35 base pairs upstream of the start). Transcription stops at a **terminator** sequence. Because there is no nucleus, ribosomes can begin translating the mRNA while it is still being made.
- In **eukaryotes**, RNA polymerase II transcribes protein-coding genes and needs **general transcription factors** to bind the promoter, many of which recognise the **TATA box**. The first product, **pre-mRNA**, is processed in the nucleus before export:
  1. A **5′ cap** (a modified guanine nucleotide) is added, protecting the mRNA and helping ribosomes bind.
  2. A **poly-A tail** of about 100–250 adenine nucleotides is added to the 3′ end, increasing stability.
  3. **Splicing** by the **spliceosome** removes **introns** (non-coding regions) and joins **exons**. **Alternative splicing** joins exons in different combinations, so one gene can produce several proteins.

### Translation

**Translation** uses the mRNA sequence to build a polypeptide on a **ribosome**. The **genetic code** reads mRNA in **codons** of three bases. There are 64 codons: 61 code for amino acids and 3 are stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA). AUG codes for methionine and is the usual **start codon**. The code is **degenerate** (most amino acids have more than one codon), **unambiguous** (each codon means one amino acid) and nearly **universal**.

**Transfer RNA (tRNA)** molecules act as adaptors. Each carries an **anticodon** that pairs with a codon, and the matching amino acid on its 3′ end. Enzymes called **aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases** attach the correct amino acid to each tRNA, using ATP; these enzymes are what actually enforce the code. Flexible pairing at the third codon position (**wobble**) lets some tRNAs read more than one codon.

The ribosome has three tRNA binding sites: **A** (aminoacyl, where new tRNAs enter), **P** (peptidyl, holding the growing chain) and **E** (exit).

1. **Initiation** — the small subunit binds the mRNA (in bacteria at the **Shine–Dalgarno sequence**; in eukaryotes at the 5′ cap, then scanning to the first AUG). The initiator tRNA carrying methionine pairs with AUG in the P site, and the large subunit joins.
2. **Elongation** — a tRNA matching the next codon enters the A site. The ribosome's rRNA catalyses a **peptide bond** between the chain in the P site and the new amino acid (the rRNA acts as a **ribozyme**). The ribosome then moves along one codon (**translocation**), shifting tRNAs from A to P to E. Elongation uses GTP.
3. **Termination** — when a stop codon reaches the A site, a **release factor** binds and the polypeptide is released.

### Gene regulation in prokaryotes: the lac operon

An **operon** is a cluster of genes under one promoter and transcribed together, controlled by an **operator** sequence. The ***lac* operon** of *E. coli* contains three genes for using lactose, including *lacZ* (β-galactosidase).

- **No lactose:** a **repressor** protein (made from the separate *lacI* gene) binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. The operon is off.
- **Lactose present:** a form of lactose (allolactose) binds the repressor and changes its shape, so it releases the operator. The operon is **inducible**.
- **Glucose also matters:** when glucose is low, cAMP levels rise; cAMP binds the **catabolite activator protein (CAP)**, which binds near the promoter and strongly boosts transcription. When glucose is present, cAMP is low and transcription stays low even with lactose.

So the *lac* operon is fully on only when lactose is present **and** glucose is absent. This saves energy by using glucose first.

By contrast, the *trp* operon (for making tryptophan) is **repressible**: tryptophan binds and activates its repressor, switching off synthesis when tryptophan is plentiful.

### Gene regulation in eukaryotes

Eukaryotic genes are controlled at many levels:

- **Chromatin** — tightly packed chromatin (heterochromatin) is inaccessible. **Histone acetylation** loosens packing and usually activates genes; **DNA methylation** of promoters usually silences them.
- **Transcription** — **specific transcription factors** (**activators** and **repressors**) bind **enhancers** and **silencers**, which can be thousands of base pairs from the gene. DNA loops so that proteins on enhancers contact the promoter machinery. Each cell type's combination of transcription factors determines its pattern of gene expression.
- **RNA processing** — alternative splicing.
- **mRNA stability and translation** — **microRNAs** bind complementary mRNAs and block translation or cause breakdown.
- **Protein level** — modification (such as phosphorylation) and controlled breakdown.

### Mutations

A **mutation** is a permanent change in DNA sequence. Causes include replication errors and **mutagens** such as UV light (which forms thymine dimers), ionising radiation and some chemicals. Mutations in germ-line cells can be inherited; **somatic** mutations affect only the individual.

**Point mutations** (single base substitutions) have different effects:

| Type | Effect on codon | Effect on protein |
|---|---|---|
| **Silent** | Codes for the same amino acid | None |
| **Missense** | Codes for a different amino acid | Ranges from none to severe |
| **Nonsense** | Creates a stop codon | Shortened, usually non-functional protein |

**Frameshift** mutations are insertions or deletions of a number of bases that is not a multiple of three. They change the **reading frame**, altering every codon after the mutation and often creating an early stop codon. An insertion or deletion of three bases adds or removes one amino acid without shifting the frame.

Larger **chromosomal mutations** include deletions, duplications, inversions and translocations of chromosome segments.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: from DNA to protein

The template strand of part of a gene reads: `3′-TAC GGA TTC ACT-5′`

1. The mRNA is complementary to the template and antiparallel: `5′-AUG CCU AAG UGA-3′`.
2. The coding strand matches the mRNA with T for U: `5′-ATG CCT AAG TGA-3′`.
3. Translate using the codon table: AUG = Met, CCU = Pro, AAG = Lys, UGA = stop.
4. Polypeptide: **Met–Pro–Lys**.

### Example 2: classifying mutations

Using the same template, predict the effect of each change.

- Template base 6 changes from A to G (`TAC GGG TTC ACT`). mRNA codon 2 becomes CCC, which still codes Pro. **Silent**.
- Template base 7 changes from T to A (`TAC GGA ATC ACT`). mRNA codon 3 becomes UAG, a stop codon. **Nonsense**: the polypeptide is just Met–Pro.
- A G is inserted after template base 3 (`TAC GGG ATT CAC T`). mRNA reads AUG CCC UAA..., so codon 3 becomes a stop. **Frameshift**, causing early termination.

### Example 3: predicting lac operon expression

What is β-galactosidase production in each condition?

| Condition | Repressor on operator? | CAP–cAMP bound? | Transcription |
|---|---|---|---|
| Glucose, no lactose | Yes | No | Off |
| Glucose + lactose | No | No | Low |
| No glucose, lactose | No | Yes | High |
| No glucose, no lactose | Yes | Yes | Off |

A mutant whose repressor cannot bind the operator would produce enzyme in all conditions (high or low depending on glucose). This is **constitutive** expression.

## Common mistakes

- Saying DNA polymerase builds 3′ → 5′. New strands are always made 5′ → 3′; the template is read 3′ → 5′.
- Confusing template and coding strands. The mRNA matches the coding strand (with U), not the template.
- Writing anticodons when asked for codons, or forgetting to replace T with U in RNA.
- Thinking the lac operon is switched on by lactose alone. Glucose must also be low for strong transcription.
- Assuming every point mutation changes the protein. Many are silent because of degeneracy.

## Exam tips

- In sequence questions, label 5′ and 3′ ends on every strand you write, and use the codon table carefully.
- For replication, link each enzyme to its exact job and explain why the lagging strand is discontinuous using "antiparallel" and "5′ → 3′".
- Operon questions often use mutants (repressor, operator or promoter). Work out which protein can or cannot bind, then predict expression.
- When explaining a mutation's effect, connect DNA → mRNA codon → amino acid → protein shape → function.

## Tips to remember

- **"New DNA grows from its tail: 5′ → 3′, always"**: DNA polymerase can only add to a free 3′–OH. Picture a train that can only add carriages at the back.
- **The leading strand leads, the lagging strand lags behind in bits**: because the strands are antiparallel, only one strand can be made continuously toward the fork; the other is made in Okazaki fragments, each with its own RNA primer, later joined by ligase.
- **The replication crew: "Help Stop That Primer, Please Link"** (made-up memory trick): **H**elicase unwinds, **S**ingle-strand binding proteins hold strands apart, **T**opoisomerase relieves twisting, **P**rimase lays primers, DNA **P**olymerase builds (III) and swaps primers for DNA (I), **L**igase seals.
- **mRNA is a copy of the coding strand, not the template**: write the coding strand, swap T for U, and you have the mRNA. Codons are on mRNA; anticodons are on tRNA.
- **lac operon in one line: "Lactose lifts the lock (repressor), low glucose lights the lamp (CAP–cAMP)."** It is fully on only when lactose is present and glucose is absent.
- **"Silent, Missense, Nonsense, Frameshift" go from mildest to usually worst**: same amino acid, different amino acid, stop codon, every codon after the change scrambled. Quick check: an insertion or deletion of three bases does not shift the frame.

## Key terms

- **Semi-conservative replication** — each new DNA molecule has one old and one new strand.
- **Okazaki fragment** — short DNA segment made on the lagging strand.
- **Primer** — short RNA sequence that provides a 3′ end for DNA polymerase.
- **Promoter** — DNA sequence where RNA polymerase binds to start transcription.
- **Intron** — non-coding sequence removed from pre-mRNA by splicing.
- **Codon** — three-base mRNA sequence specifying an amino acid or stop.
- **Anticodon** — three-base tRNA sequence that pairs with a codon.
- **Operon** — group of bacterial genes transcribed together under one promoter and operator.
- **Enhancer** — eukaryotic DNA sequence that binds activators to increase transcription.
- **Frameshift mutation** — insertion or deletion that changes the reading frame.

## Summary

- DNA replication is semi-conservative; helicase, primase, DNA polymerase and ligase work together, with continuous leading and discontinuous lagging strands.
- Transcription makes RNA 5′ → 3′ from the template strand; eukaryotic pre-mRNA is capped, tailed and spliced.
- Translation reads codons on ribosomes, with tRNAs delivering amino acids through the A, P and E sites.
- The lac operon is induced by lactose and boosted by CAP–cAMP when glucose is low.
- Eukaryotes regulate genes through chromatin, transcription factors, splicing, microRNAs and protein modification.
- Mutations may be silent, missense, nonsense or frameshift, with effects ranging from none to complete loss of function.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand?
questions.explanation: DNA ligase forms the final phosphodiester bonds joining fragments. Primase (A) is tempting because it is also linked to Okazaki fragments, but it makes the RNA primers that start each one.

questions.prompt: Which ribosome site holds the tRNA attached to the growing polypeptide chain?
questions.explanation: The P (peptidyl) site holds the tRNA carrying the growing chain. The A site (A) receives incoming aminoacyl-tRNAs, and the Shine–Dalgarno sequence is part of bacterial mRNA, not a ribosome site.

questions.prompt: Why is the lagging strand synthesised as discontinuous fragments?

options.A: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to a 3′ end, and the lagging template runs in the opposite direction to fork movement
options.B: Helicase can only unwind short sections of the lagging strand at a time
options.C: The lagging strand contains introns that must be skipped
options.D: Primase cannot bind to the leading strand

questions.explanation: Because the strands are antiparallel and synthesis is only 5′ → 3′, one new strand must be made away from the fork in short pieces. Option D is wrong because the leading strand also needs a primer, just only one at the start.

questions.prompt: E. coli is grown in a medium containing both glucose and lactose. Which statement best describes transcription of the lac operon?

options.A: High, because lactose has removed the repressor
options.B: Off, because the repressor is bound to the operator
options.C: Low, because the repressor is released but CAP–cAMP is not bound as cAMP levels are low

questions.explanation: Lactose (as allolactose) releases the repressor, but glucose keeps cAMP low, so CAP cannot boost transcription. Option A overlooks the need for CAP–cAMP, and D reverses the effect of glucose.

questions.prompt: How can one eukaryotic gene code for several different proteins?

options.A: Different tRNAs read the codons differently in each cell type
options.B: Alternative splicing joins different combinations of exons into the mature mRNA
options.C: The gene is replicated differently in each tissue
options.D: The poly-A tail is translated into extra amino acids

questions.explanation: Alternative splicing includes or skips particular exons, giving different mRNAs and proteins from one gene. Option A is wrong because the genetic code is unambiguous: a codon means the same amino acid in every cell.

questions.prompt: A DNA template strand reads 3′-TAC CAT GGA-5′. What is the sequence of the mRNA produced?
questions.explanation: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template and uses U instead of T: 5′-AUG GUA CCU-3′. Option B is the coding DNA strand (with T), and C has the right bases but the ends labelled the wrong way round.

questions.prompt: A mutation changes an mRNA codon from UAC (tyrosine) to UAA. What type of mutation is this, and what is its likely effect?

options.A: Nonsense; the polypeptide is shortened at this point
options.B: Missense; tyrosine is replaced by another amino acid
options.D: Frameshift; every following codon is changed

questions.explanation: UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends early, producing a truncated, usually non-functional protein. Option D is wrong because a single substitution does not change the reading frame; only insertions or deletions do.

questions.prompt: A mutant E. coli strain produces β-galactosidase even when no lactose is present. Which mutation would most likely cause this?

options.A: A mutation in the promoter that prevents RNA polymerase binding
options.B: A mutation in the operator that prevents the repressor from binding
options.C: A mutation that stops CAP binding cAMP
options.D: A mutation in lacZ that creates a stop codon

questions.explanation: If the repressor cannot bind the operator, the operon cannot be switched off, so it is expressed constitutively. Options A and C would reduce expression, and D would prevent active enzyme being made at all.
